title: 2026 United States House of Representatives Election in South Dakota's At-Large District
description: This election will determine South Dakota's sole U.S. House representative, a seat being vacated by four-term incumbent Dusty Johnson, who is running for governor. Republican nominee Marty Jackley, the state's attorney general and a former U.S. attorney, faces Democratic nominee Nikki Gronli, a former USDA Rural Development state director and small business owner. South Dakota is a heavily Republican state — the GOP has held this seat since 2011 — and the race is rated as Safe Republican by major nonpartisan forecasters. The primary elections were held on June 2, 2026; Jackley won the Republican primary with 79% of the vote, while Gronli was unopposed in the Democratic primary.
polling_note: No general election polls were found for this race. Primary polls showed Jackley leading Bialota by wide margins; general election polling has not been conducted publicly as of mid-2026. The race is rated 'Solid R' by Cook Political Report, 'Safe R' by Sabato's Crystal Ball, and 'Solid R' by Inside Elections.

candidates.name: Marty Jackley
candidates.summary: Marty Jackley is the South Dakota Attorney General (2009–2019, 2023–present) and a former U.S. Attorney for the District of South Dakota. He won the June 2, 2026 Republican primary with 79.2% of the vote to claim the nomination for South Dakota's at-large U.S. House seat. Jackley has emphasized his conservative record on crime, life, and the Second Amendment, and has been endorsed by U.S. House Republican leadership.

candidates.name: Nikki Gronli
candidates.summary: Nikki Gronli is the Democratic nominee for South Dakota's U.S. House seat, running unopposed in the June 2, 2026 primary. She previously served as USDA Rural Development state director for South Dakota (2022–2025) and as vice chair of the South Dakota Democratic Party. Gronli is a small business owner and president of Flatlander Strategies, and her campaign focuses on rural economic development, healthcare access, and opposition to tariffs that she argues hurt South Dakota farmers.
